subject: SCIENCE
title: Classify the Animals
objective: Classify animals by observable traits and explain the chosen rule.
introduction: Milo sorts animals into groups. Can you sort them by what you can see, like feathers or no feathers?

vocabulary.definition: To sort things into groups that are alike.
A living thing that can move and needs food.
A feature or quality a living thing has.

activities.instruction: Watch and listen — Milo shows how to sort animals by what you see.
activities.content: A learner-made group is an observation tool, not formal biological taxonomy.

feedback.correct: Nice work. Continue to the next step.

activities.accessibilityAlternative: Text alternative: A learner-made group is an observation tool, not formal biological taxonomy.

activities.instruction: Tap each example and read what it shows.
activities.accessibilityAlternative: A numbered list of the same examples is available for keyboard and screen-reader use.

activities.instruction: Sort each card: does it follow the chosen grouping rule?

feedback.correct: Great sorting! Your groups are correct.
feedback.retry: Use the explanation, not color or position.

activities.accessibilityAlternative: Tap an item and then tap a labeled category; dragging is optional.

activities.instruction: Which rule uses an observable trait?

feedback.correct: Correct: has feathers or no feathers
feedback.retry: Look again — luck and niceness are not observable. Tap the trait you can see! 💪

activities.accessibilityAlternative: All choices are visible text and selectable with TalkBack.

activities.instruction: Match each trait to its group.

feedback.retry: Return to the explanation and compare one pair at a time.

activities.accessibilityAlternative: A list-based matching control replaces drag gestures.

activities.instruction: Put the steps in order: pick a trait, sort, say the rule.

feedback.correct: You are ready for the five-question check.

activities.accessibilityAlternative: Up and down buttons provide an alternative to dragging.

items.prompt: Which statement about grouping animals is true?

options.text: Sorting animals by what you see is a way to observe, not a scientist's official name.

items.explanation: Groups you make from what you see help you observe animals. They are not official scientific names, and grouping by your favorite color is not about the animal.

items.prompt: Which grouping rule uses a trait you can see?
items.explanation: You can see whether an animal has feathers, so that rule uses an observable trait. Luck and niceness cannot be seen.

items.prompt: Which grouping rule is NOT about the animal?
items.explanation: Grouping by your favorite color is about your likes, not the animal. Feathers and how an animal moves are traits you can observe.

items.prompt: Which rule uses an observable trait?
items.explanation: You can see feathers, so it is an observable trait. Luck and niceness cannot be seen on an animal.

items.prompt: Which rule groups animals by something you can see?
items.explanation: Scales are visible, so it is an observable trait. Invisible traits and favorite colors cannot be seen on the animal.
